title: Present routines and time expressions: cumulative review
objectives: Use common prepositions with routine time expressions.
Describe a weekly routine with appropriate present simple forms.
Review questions, be and frequency adverbs from earlier units.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A routine is something a person does regularly. We can describe a routine with the present simple and add a time expression to say when it happens. ‘I have breakfast at seven’ gives a clock time. ‘I visit my family on Sundays’ tells us the day. These expressions help a listener understand the pattern of a person’s week.

This unit also reviews the earlier units. You will use be to describe a situation, the present simple to describe actions, do or does to ask questions, and frequency words to say how often something happens. Think about the meaning and the subject before you choose the verb.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Use at before a clock time: at six, at 8.30 or at half past nine. Use on before a day or a day with a part of the day: on Monday, on Fridays and on Tuesday evening. Use in with parts of the day such as the morning, the afternoon and the evening. A common exception is at night. ‘At the weekend’ is common in British English; ‘on the weekend’ is common in American English.

Time expressions often come at the end: ‘We study in the evening’. They can also come at the beginning, followed by a comma in writing: ‘On Fridays, we study together.’ An expression beginning with every does not normally need at, on or in: ‘every Monday’, not ‘on every Monday’ in this routine pattern.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Read the examples below as parts of a weekly diary. The verb still agrees with the subject: ‘She starts at nine’, but ‘They start at nine’. In a negative, use the base form after don’t or doesn’t: ‘She doesn’t work on Sundays’. In a question, put do or does before the subject: ‘Does she work on Sundays?’

Frequency adverbs such as usually normally come before an ordinary main verb but after be: ‘I usually eat at home’ and ‘I am usually at home at six’. Longer expressions such as twice a week often come at the end. More than one time expression can appear together: ‘We meet at seven on Mondays.’

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Do not use in before a weekday in this pattern: say ‘on Monday’. Do not use on before a clock time: say ‘at seven’. A day and a time need their own prepositions: ‘at six on Friday’. Some expressions have other uses and meanings in English, so learn these examples in their routine context rather than treating every preposition as a universal rule.

Be and ordinary verbs use different question patterns. Ask ‘Are you busy on Fridays?’ with be, but ‘Do you work on Fridays?’ with an ordinary verb. This review connects the forms; the exercises identify which earlier units they revisit.

examples.note: Use at with a clock time.

examples.sentence: I visit my friend on Tuesdays.
examples.note: Use on with a day of the week.
Use at in the expression at night.

examples.sentence: On Fridays, Leo finishes work early.
examples.note: A time expression can come at the beginning.

examples.sentence: She usually works at the weekend.
examples.note: At the weekend is a common British expression.

examples.sentence: They don’t study on Sunday evenings.
examples.note: Use don’t and the base verb with they.

examples.sentence: Are you busy at six? Yes, I am.
examples.note: Use be in the question and positive short answer.

common_errors.correct: I have a class on Monday.

common_errors.reason: Use at before a clock time.
Use the base form after doesn’t.

summary: Use at for clock times, on for days and in for the morning, afternoon and evening.
Use at night and every Monday without an extra preposition.
Check the subject, verb and position of frequency adverbs when describing routines.
